chapters.title: Real Numbers
chapters.summary: This chapter builds the number system on the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every composite number factors uniquely into primes. You learn to find HCF and LCM by prime factorisation, use the identity HCF x LCM = product of two numbers, prove that sqrt(2), sqrt(3) and sqrt(5) are irrational, and classify decimal expansions as terminating or non-terminating recurring. Note that Euclid's division lemma has been removed from the rationalised syllabus, so revision time should go to factorisation, irrationality proofs and decimal tests.
hotTopics: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
HCF and LCM by prime factorisation
HCF x LCM = product of two numbers
Irrationality proofs of sqrt(2), sqrt(3), sqrt(5)
Terminating and non-terminating recurring decimals
Word problems on bells, ropes and beads

sections.heading: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
points: Every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique apart from the order in which the primes appear; this statement is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.
Example: 84 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 7 = 2^2 x 3 x 7; no other collection of primes can multiply to give 84.
A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself; primes are the building blocks from which every composite number is made.
The theorem rests on a key lemma: if a prime p divides the product ab, then p must divide a or p must divide b.
HCF is the product of the common primes taken with their smallest powers, while LCM is the product of all primes involved taken with their greatest powers.
Trees and repeated division both work: keep splitting a number until only primes remain at the ends of the branches.

keyTerms.meaning: Every composite number has a unique prime factorisation, ignoring the order of factors.
Writing a number as a product of primes, e.g. 156 = 2^2 x 3 x 13.
A number with more than two factors.

sections.trick: Factor tree habit: split, split, split until every leaf is prime; the same primes must appear for any tree you draw, only the order changes.
sections.examPointer: CBSE asks 1-2 mark questions to express a number as a product of primes and to factorise three numbers; always show the factorisation line by line because method marks are given for the working.

sections.heading: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
points: HCF (Highest Common Factor) = product of the primes common to both numbers, each taken with the smallest power, e.g. 12 = 2^2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3^2 give HCF = 2 x 3 = 6.
LCM (Lowest Common Multiple) = product of all primes involved, each taken with the greatest power, e.g. LCM(12, 18) = 2^2 x 3^2 = 36.

Worked example with steps: find the HCF and LCM of 6 and 20. Step 1: 6 = 2 x 3 and 20 = 2^2 x 5. Step 2: HCF = common prime with lowest power = 2. Step 3: LCM = 2^2 x 3 x 5 = 60. Step 4: check that 6 x 20 = 120 = 2 x 60.
For three numbers a, b, c the HCF uses only the primes present in all three factorisations, while the LCM takes every prime at its highest power.
For small numbers, listing factors or multiples also works, but prime factorisation is the fastest and safest route in the board exam.

keyTerms.meaning: Highest Common Factor: the largest number dividing all the given numbers.
Lowest Common Multiple: the smallest number divisible by all the given numbers.
Numbers whose HCF is 1, e.g. 8 and 15.

sections.trick: Remember the chant: HCF = Common primes, Lowest powers; LCM = List all primes, mOst (highest) powers.
sections.examPointer: A favourite 2-3 mark question: find the HCF and LCM of two or three numbers and verify HCF x LCM = product of the two numbers; write the verification line explicitly to earn the last mark.

sections.heading: HCF x LCM = Product of Two Numbers
points: For any two positive integers a and b: HCF(a, b) x LCM(a, b) = a x b; this identity is the most used formula of the chapter.
The identity fails for three numbers: LCM(6, 72, 120) = 360 but 6 x 72 x 120 = 51840, which is not HCF x LCM of the triple since HCF(6, 72, 120) x 360 = 2160 only.
Rearrangements are common: if HCF and LCM and one number are given, the other number = (HCF x LCM) / known number.
Application guide: the least number divisible by each of a and b is the LCM, the greatest number dividing each is the HCF, and events that repeat together recur after the LCM of their intervals.

keyTerms.meaning: HCF(a, b) x LCM(a, b) = a x b, valid only for a pair of numbers.
Bells, lights or runners that start together and repeat at fixed intervals meet again after the LCM of the intervals.

sections.trick: HCF is always a factor of the LCM; if your HCF does not divide your LCM, recheck the factorisation before moving on.
sections.examPointer: Often asked in one step: given the HCF, LCM and one number, find the other; quote the identity HCF x LCM = a x b before substituting to show the reasoning.

sections.heading: Revisiting Irrational Numbers
points: Irrational numbers cannot be written as p/q where p and q are integers and q is not 0; their decimal expansions are non-terminating and non-repeating.
Key results of the chapter: sqrt(2), sqrt(3) and sqrt(5) are irrational; also p + q x sqrt(r) is irrational whenever p, q are non-zero rationals and sqrt(r) is irrational.

Proof pattern for sqrt(2): assume sqrt(2) = a/b with a, b coprime; squaring gives a^2 = 2b^2, so 2 divides a; write a = 2c, then 4c^2 = 2b^2 gives b^2 = 2c^2, so 2 divides b; this contradicts a and b being coprime, hence sqrt(2) is irrational.
Sum or difference of a rational and an irrational number is always irrational; product or quotient of a non-zero rational and an irrational is also irrational.
Sum of two irrationals may be rational or irrational (sqrt(2) + (-sqrt(2)) = 0), so never claim it is always irrational.

keyTerms.meaning: A real number that cannot be expressed as p/q with integers p and q not 0.
Assume the opposite of the result, derive an impossibility, and conclude the result is true.
Integers whose only common positive factor is 1.

sections.trick: Irrationality proofs are always contradiction proofs: assume p/q with coprime p, q, force the prime to divide p, then force it to divide q, and end with the line that this contradicts coprimality.
sections.examPointer: Three-mark favourites: prove sqrt(3), sqrt(5) or 3 + 2sqrt(5) irrational; always open with the assumption and close with the contradiction sentence, since both carry marks.

sections.heading: Decimal Expansions of Rational Numbers
points: Theorem: let x = p/q be a rational number in its lowest terms; if the denominator q = 2^n x 5^m (only 2s and 5s), then p/q has a terminating decimal expansion.
If the reduced denominator contains any prime other than 2 or 5, the expansion is non-terminating recurring.
Worked example: 13/3125 = 13/(5^5); multiply numerator and denominator by 2^5 = 32 to get 416/10^5 = 0.00416, a terminating decimal.
Worked example: 17/6 has reduced denominator 2 x 3; the leftover 3 means 17/6 = 2.8333... is non-terminating recurring.
Reduce to lowest terms before testing: 6/12 looks like it has denominator 12 = 2^2 x 3, but 6/12 = 1/2 = 0.5 terminates.

keyTerms.meaning: A decimal expansion that ends after finitely many digits, possible exactly when the reduced denominator is 2^n x 5^m.
A decimal expansion in which a block of digits repeats forever, e.g. 2.8333...
The fraction form p/q in which p and q have HCF 1.

sections.trick: Simplify first, then inspect the denominator: only 2s and 5s terminate, any other prime means recurring.
sections.examPointer: 1-2 mark questions ask whether the expansion of a given fraction terminates or recurs without actual division; answer with the denominator condition quoted word for word.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Exam Tips (Real Numbers)
points: Mistake: applying HCF x LCM = product to three numbers; the identity holds only for two numbers.
Mistake: claiming 6^n can end in 0; since 6^n = 2^n x 3^n has no prime factor 5, it is never divisible by 10.
Mistake: in irrationality proofs, forgetting to state that a and b are coprime at the start, or skipping the second divisibility step on b.
Mistake: testing the terminating condition on the given denominator instead of the reduced denominator.
Tip: in word problems, bells and traffic lights together need the LCM, while maximum length of rope, tile or string needs the HCF.
Tip: complete 2-mark answers with a verification line; CBSE awards method marks for correct factorisation lines even if arithmetic slips later.

keyTerms.meaning: a divides b if b = a x k for some integer k.
The proof ending where the assumption leads to an impossible conclusion.

sections.trick: Two phrases decide the whole word problem: greatest that divides means HCF, smallest that is divisible means LCM.
sections.examPointer: Expect a mix in the paper: one computation on HCF and LCM, one irrationality proof and one case-style or word problem; practise writing proofs in full sentences.

mcqs.question: The HCF of 12 and 18 is:
mcqs.explanation: 12 = 2^2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3^2; the common primes with the lowest powers give 2 x 3 = 6.

mcqs.question: Every positive odd integer is of the form:
mcqs.explanation: Odd numbers leave remainder 1 on division by 2, so every odd positive integer is 2m + 1 for some whole number m; 4m + 3 covers only part of the odds.

mcqs.question: The LCM of 5 and 20 is:
mcqs.explanation: 20 = 2^2 x 5 already contains the prime 5, so the LCM is 20; indeed 20 is divisible by both 5 and 20.

mcqs.question: The product of a non-zero rational number and an irrational number is:
mcqs.explanation: If r is non-zero rational, s irrational and rs = q were rational, then s = q/r would be rational, a contradiction; hence the product is always irrational.

mcqs.question: The HCF of 96 and 404 is:
mcqs.explanation: 96 = 2^5 x 3 and 404 = 2^2 x 101; the only common prime is 2 with lowest power 2, so HCF = 4.

mcqs.question: If HCF(a, b) = 5 and a x b = 150, then LCM(a, b) equals:
mcqs.explanation: Using HCF x LCM = a x b: LCM = 150 / 5 = 30.

mcqs.question: The decimal expansion of 13/3125 is:
mcqs.explanation: 3125 = 5^5; multiply numerator and denominator by 2^5 = 32 to get (13 x 32)/10^5 = 416/100000 = 0.00416, which terminates.

mcqs.question: The largest number that divides 245 and 1029 leaving remainder 5 in each case is:
mcqs.explanation: Required number = HCF(245 - 5, 1029 - 5) = HCF(240, 1024); since 240 = 16 x 15 and 1024 = 16 x 64, the answer is 16.

mcqs.question: The LCM of 6, 72 and 120 is:
mcqs.explanation: 6 = 2 x 3, 72 = 2^3 x 3^2, 120 = 2^3 x 3 x 5; taking every prime at its highest power gives LCM = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5 = 360.

mcqs.question: Given that HCF(306, 657) = 9, the LCM of 306 and 657 is:

boardQuestions.question: Use the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic to find the HCF and LCM of 26 and 91.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Factorise 26 = 2 x 13. Step 2: Factorise 91 = 7 x 13. Step 3: HCF = product of the common primes = 13. Step 4: LCM = 2 x 7 x 13 = 182. Step 5: Verify: 26 x 91 = 2366 and 13 x 182 = 2366, so HCF x LCM = product of the numbers. Answer: HCF = 13 and LCM = 182.

boardQuestions.question: Check whether 6^n can end with the digit 0 for any natural number n.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Any number ending in 0 must be divisible by 10 = 2 x 5, so its prime factorisation must contain both 2 and 5. Step 2: 6^n = (2 x 3)^n = 2^n x 3^n. Step 3: The only primes appearing are 2 and 3; the prime 5 never appears. Step 4: Since 5 is not a factor, 6^n is never divisible by 10. Answer: 6^n cannot end with the digit 0 for any natural number n.

boardQuestions.question: Prove that sqrt(3) is an irrational number.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Assume sqrt(3) is rational, so sqrt(3) = a/b where a and b are coprime integers and b is not 0. Step 2: Squaring both sides gives a^2 = 3b^2, so 3 divides a^2. Step 3: Since 3 is prime, 3 divides a; write a = 3c for some integer c. Step 4: Substituting, 9c^2 = 3b^2 gives b^2 = 3c^2, so 3 divides b^2 and hence 3 divides b. Step 5: Now 3 divides both a and b, which contradicts the fact that a and b are coprime. Step 6: Our assumption is wrong. Answer: sqrt(3) is irrational.

boardQuestions.question: Prove that 3 + 2sqrt(5) is an irrational number, given that sqrt(5) is irrational.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Assume 3 + 2sqrt(5) is rational and equal to some rational number r. Step 2: Then 2sqrt(5) = r - 3, which is rational because the difference of two rationals is rational. Step 3: Dividing by 2, sqrt(5) = (r - 3)/2, which is also rational. Step 4: This contradicts the given fact that sqrt(5) is irrational. Step 5: The assumption must be false. Answer: 3 + 2sqrt(5) is irrational.

boardQuestions.question: Find the HCF and LCM of 96 and 404 by prime factorisation and verify that HCF x LCM = 96 x 404.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: 96 = 2^5 x 3. Step 2: 404 = 2^2 x 101. Step 3: HCF = 2^2 = 4 (common prime, lowest power). Step 4: LCM = 2^5 x 3 x 101 = 9696 (all primes, highest powers). Step 5: HCF x LCM = 4 x 9696 = 38784. Step 6: 96 x 404 = 38784. Answer: HCF = 4, LCM = 9696, and the identity HCF x LCM = product of the two numbers is verified.

boardQuestions.question: Three bells toll at intervals of 9, 12 and 15 minutes respectively. If they all toll together at 8:00 am, after how many minutes will they toll together again, and at what time?
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: The bells toll together again after LCM(9, 12, 15) minutes. Step 2: 9 = 3^2, 12 = 2^2 x 3, 15 = 3 x 5. Step 3: LCM = 2^2 x 3^2 x 5 = 180 minutes. Step 4: 180 minutes = 3 hours, so 8:00 am plus 3 hours is 11:00 am. Answer: the bells toll together again after 180 minutes, at 11:00 am.

boardQuestions.question: A craft teacher has 96 red beads, 240 blue beads and 336 green beads. She wants to string all the beads into identical strings so that each string contains the same number of beads of a single colour, with no bead left over. (a) Find the greatest number of strings she can make. (b) How many beads of each colour will one string contain? (c) How many strings will be blue?
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: The greatest number of strings = HCF(96, 240, 336), since each string must take an equal share of every colour. Step 2: 96 = 2^5 x 3, 240 = 2^4 x 3 x 5, 336 = 2^4 x 3 x 7. Step 3: HCF = 2^4 x 3 = 48, so 48 strings can be made. Step 4: Red beads per string = 96/48 = 2, blue = 240/48 = 5, green = 336/48 = 7. Step 5: Number of blue strings = 240/48 = 5. Answer: (a) 48 strings, (b) 2 red, 5 blue and 7 green beads per string, (c) 5 blue strings.

chapters.title: Polynomials
chapters.summary: This chapter connects algebra to graphs: the zeroes of a polynomial are exactly the x-coordinates where its graph meets the x-axis. The focus is on quadratic polynomials: finding zeroes by factorisation, using the relationships sum of zeroes = -b/a and product of zeroes = c/a, and building a polynomial from its zeroes. The division algorithm for polynomials and the relationships for cubic polynomials are excluded from the rationalised syllabus.
hotTopics: Geometrical meaning of zeroes from graphs
Sum and product of zeroes (alpha-beta relations)
Forming a quadratic polynomial from its zeroes
Finding unknown coefficients k
Symmetric expressions in the zeroes
Parabola shapes and number of zeroes

sections.heading: Zeroes of a Polynomial
points: A zero of a polynomial p(x) is a number c for which p(c) = 0; for example, the zero of p(x) = x - 5 is 5 because 5 - 5 = 0.
If k is a zero of p(x), then (x - k) is a factor of p(x); conversely, if (x - k) is a factor, then k is a zero.

Worked example with steps: find the zeroes of p(x) = x^2 - 5x + 6. Step 1: factorise as (x - 2)(x - 3). Step 2: set each factor equal to 0. Step 3: the zeroes are x = 2 and x = 3. Step 4: check p(2) = 4 - 10 + 6 = 0 and p(3) = 9 - 15 + 6 = 0.
A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes, since its graph can meet the x-axis at most n times.
A non-zero constant polynomial has no zero, while the zero polynomial has every real number as a zero.

keyTerms.meaning: A value c with p(c) = 0.
A polynomial that divides p(x) exactly; (x - k) is a factor exactly when k is a zero.
The highest power of the variable in the polynomial.

sections.trick: Zero means output zero: put p(c) = 0 and solve; every zero k pairs with a factor (x - k), so counting factors counts zeroes.
sections.examPointer: One-mark questions ask for the zero of a linear polynomial or the maximum number of zeroes of a cubic; answer in one line with a quick substitution as verification.

sections.heading: Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes
points: The zeroes of a polynomial are exactly the x-coordinates of the points where its graph intersects the x-axis.
A linear polynomial ax + b has a straight-line graph that cuts the x-axis at exactly one point, so it has exactly one zero, namely -b/a.

A quadratic polynomial ax^2 + bx + c has a parabola that opens upwards when a > 0 and downwards when a < 0; it can cut the x-axis at 2 points (2 zeroes), touch it at 1 point (1 zero) or not meet it at all (no real zero).
A cubic polynomial graph meets the x-axis at 1, 2 or 3 points, so a cubic always has at least one real zero and at most three.
Worked mini-example: the parabola y = x^2 - 4 meets the x-axis where x^2 - 4 = 0, that is at x = 2 and x = -2, so it has two zeroes.

keyTerms.meaning: A point where the graph crosses the x-axis; its x-coordinate is a zero of the polynomial.
The U-shaped graph of a quadratic polynomial.
A degree 3 polynomial whose graph always crosses the x-axis at least once.

sections.trick: Count zeroes by counting x-axis meetings: cuts twice = 2 zeroes, touches once = 1 zero, never meets = no real zeroes.
sections.examPointer: Graph questions show a curve and ask the number of zeroes; read only the x-axis intersections, never the y-axis, and answer with a count, not the values.

sections.heading: Relationship between Zeroes and Coefficients (Quadratic)
points: For the quadratic polynomial ax^2 + bx + c (a not 0) with zeroes α and β: sum α + β = -b/a and product α x β = c/a.
Worked example: for 2x^2 - 7x + 5, α + β = 7/2 and α x β = 5/2; the actual zeroes are 1 and 5/2, and indeed 1 + 5/2 = 7/2 and 1 x 5/2 = 5/2.
Derived identities: α^2 + β^2 = (α + β)^2 - 2αβ and (α - β)^2 = (α + β)^2 - 4αβ.
Also 1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/(αβ); these symmetric expressions are evaluated without ever finding the zeroes.
Given the zeroes, the polynomial is x^2 - (sum)x + product when a = 1, and k[x^2 - (sum)x + product] for any non-zero k in general.

keyTerms.meaning: α + β = -b/a for the quadratic ax^2 + bx + c.
αβ = c/a for the quadratic ax^2 + bx + c.
An expression unchanged when α and β are swapped, such as α^2 + β^2.

sections.trick: Sign watch: the sum carries a minus (-b/a) while the product keeps the sign of c (c/a). Chant it: minus b over a, c over a.
sections.examPointer: Board questions ask for α^2 + β^2, 1/α + 1/β or a missing coefficient k; never solve the equation, just write the sum and product and substitute.

sections.heading: Forming a Quadratic Polynomial from its Zeroes
points: Given zeroes α and β, the simplest quadratic polynomial with those zeroes is x^2 - (α + β)x + αβ.
Worked example: zeroes 4 and -3 give sum = 1 and product = -12, so the polynomial is x^2 - x - 12; check by expanding (x - 4)(x + 3) = x^2 - x - 12.
Irrational zeroes such as 3 + sqrt(2) and 3 - sqrt(2) give sum = 6 and product = 9 - 2 = 7, so the polynomial is x^2 - 6x + 7.
Any non-zero multiple works equally: 2x^2 - 2x - 24 has the same zeroes as x^2 - x - 12, so a family of answers is correct.
For reciprocal zeroes r and 1/r, the product is 1, so the polynomial is x^2 - (r + 1/r)x + 1.

keyTerms.meaning: A polynomial whose leading coefficient is 1; the simplest member of the zero family.
A pair like 3 + sqrt(2) and 3 - sqrt(2) whose sum and product are both rational.
A three-term polynomial such as the standard quadratic x^2 - Sx + P.

sections.trick: Build it as x^2 - (sum)x + (product); the x term is always minus the sum, no exceptions.
sections.examPointer: A 2-3 mark staple: form the polynomial when zeroes are given, often as surds like 2 + sqrt(3); present it in three lines: sum, product, final polynomial.

sections.heading: Finding Unknown Coefficients
points: Strategy: translate every given condition into α + β = -b/a and αβ = c/a, then solve the resulting equation for the unknown coefficient.

Worked example: the zeroes of x^2 - 6x + k satisfy α^2 + β^2 = 40. Step 1: α + β = 6 and αβ = k. Step 2: (α + β)^2 - 2αβ = 40 gives 36 - 2k = 40. Step 3: k = -2. Step 4: check that x^2 - 6x - 2 has real zeroes since its discriminant 36 + 8 = 44 is positive.
If one zero is the negative of the other, then α + β = 0, which forces b = 0.
If the zeroes are reciprocals of each other, then αβ = 1, which forces c = a.
If the zeroes differ by a given value, use (α - β)^2 = (α + β)^2 - 4αβ.

keyTerms.meaning: A letter (usually k) in the polynomial to be determined from a condition on the zeroes.
A statement about the sum, product, difference or squares of the zeroes.
Verifying b^2 - 4ac is not negative so that the zeroes are real.

sections.trick: Translate the condition first: one zero negative of the other means sum 0; zeroes reciprocal means product 1; zeroes differ by 1 means use the (α - β)^2 identity.
sections.examPointer: Hard 3-5 mark questions hide the coefficient inside α^2 + β^2 or α - β; finish by quoting the discriminant to confirm real zeroes exist.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Exam Tips (Polynomials)
points: Mistake: writing the sum of zeroes as b/a instead of -b/a; the minus is non-negotiable.
Mistake: reading zeroes from a graph by looking at the y-axis; zeroes come from the x-axis intersections only.
Mistake: forming the polynomial as x^2 + (sum)x + product instead of x^2 - (sum)x + product.
Mistake: mixing the sum and product of two different quadratics in one question; label S and P for each polynomial separately.
Tip: after finding zeroes by factorisation, substitute one of them back into p(x) as a ten-second check.
Tip: the division algorithm for polynomials is deleted from the rationalised syllabus, so spend that revision time on the sum-product relations instead.

keyTerms.meaning: The trimmed NCERT and CBSE syllabus in which the division algorithm and cubic relationships are excluded.
Substituting a found zero back into the polynomial to confirm p(k) = 0.

sections.trick: SPF chant: Sum = -b/a, Product = c/a, Form = x^2 - Sx + P; say it before every polynomial question.
sections.examPointer: The guaranteed question type is a 3-marker linking the zeroes of one quadratic to the coefficients of another; keep the two polynomials written separately to avoid mixing their S and P.

mcqs.question: The zero of the polynomial p(x) = x - 5 is:
mcqs.explanation: Put x - 5 = 0, so x = 5; indeed p(5) = 5 - 5 = 0.

mcqs.question: The zeroes of x^2 - 3x + 2 are:
mcqs.explanation: x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)(x - 2), so the zeroes are 1 and 2.

mcqs.question: A quadratic polynomial can have at most:
mcqs.explanation: A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes; for degree 2 this means at most 2, seen as at most two x-axis cuts of the parabola.

mcqs.question: The graph of a quadratic polynomial is always a:
mcqs.explanation: y = ax^2 + bx + c with a not 0 traces a parabola opening upwards when a > 0 and downwards when a < 0.

mcqs.question: The sum of the zeroes of 2x^2 - 7x + 3 is:
mcqs.explanation: Sum of zeroes = -b/a = -(-7)/2 = 7/2 (and the product is c/a = 3/2).

mcqs.question: If α and β are the zeroes of x^2 - 5x + 6, then α^2 + β^2 equals:
A quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are 2 and -3 is:
mcqs.explanation: Sum = -1 and product = -6, so the polynomial is x^2 - (sum)x + product = x^2 + x - 6; check (x + 3)(x - 2) = x^2 + x - 6.

mcqs.question: If 4 is one zero of p(x) = x^2 - 2x - 8, the other zero is:
mcqs.explanation: Product of zeroes = c/a = -8, so the other zero = -8/4 = -2; indeed (x - 4)(x + 2) = x^2 - 2x - 8.

mcqs.question: If α and β are the zeroes of x^2 - 6x + k and α^2 + β^2 = 40, then k equals:
mcqs.explanation: α + β = 6 and αβ = k; (α + β)^2 - 2αβ = 40 gives 36 - 2k = 40, so k = -2; the equation x^2 - 6x - 2 = 0 then has real roots since its discriminant is 36 + 8 = 44 > 0.

mcqs.question: If the zeroes of the polynomial x^2 + (a + 1)x + b are 2 and -3, then:
mcqs.explanation: Sum of zeroes = 2 + (-3) = -1 = -(a + 1), so a + 1 = 1 and a = 0; product = 2 x (-3) = -6 = b; check x^2 + x - 6 = (x + 3)(x - 2).

boardQuestions.question: Find the zeroes of the polynomial 3x^2 - x - 4 and verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Split the middle term: 3x^2 - x - 4 = 3x^2 - 4x + 3x - 4 = x(3x - 4) + 1(3x - 4) = (3x - 4)(x + 1). Step 2: The zeroes are x = 4/3 and x = -1. Step 3: Sum = 4/3 - 1 = 1/3 and -b/a = -(-1)/3 = 1/3, verified. Step 4: Product = (4/3) x (-1) = -4/3 and c/a = -4/3, verified. Answer: the zeroes are 4/3 and -1, and both relationships hold.

boardQuestions.question: If one zero of the polynomial f(x) = 4x^2 - 8kx - 9 is the negative of the other, find the value of k.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Let the zeroes be α and -α. Step 2: Then α + (-α) = 0, so the sum of the zeroes is 0. Step 3: Sum of zeroes = -b/a = -(-8k)/4 = 2k. Step 4: Setting 2k = 0 gives k = 0. Answer: k = 0.

boardQuestions.question: If α and β are the zeroes of the polynomial x^2 - 5x + 4, find the values of α^2 + β^2 and 1/α + 1/β.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: From the coefficients, α + β = 5 and αβ = 4. Step 2: α^2 + β^2 = (α + β)^2 - 2αβ = 25 - 8 = 17. Step 3: 1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/(αβ) = 5/4. Answer: α^2 + β^2 = 17 and 1/α + 1/β = 5/4.

boardQuestions.question: Form a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are 3 + sqrt(2) and 3 - sqrt(2).
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Sum = (3 + sqrt(2)) + (3 - sqrt(2)) = 6. Step 2: Product = (3 + sqrt(2))(3 - sqrt(2)) = 9 - 2 = 7. Step 3: The polynomial is x^2 - (sum)x + product = x^2 - 6x + 7. Step 4: Check by the formula: the discriminant of x^2 - 6x + 7 is 36 - 28 = 8, so the zeroes are (6 + 2sqrt(2))/2 = 3 + sqrt(2) and (6 - 2sqrt(2))/2 = 3 - sqrt(2). Answer: the required polynomial is x^2 - 6x + 7.

boardQuestions.question: If α and β are the zeroes of the polynomial f(x) = x^2 - 5x + k such that α - β = 1, find the value of k and hence find the zeroes.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: α + β = 5 and αβ = k. Step 2: Using (α - β)^2 = (α + β)^2 - 4αβ, we get 1 = 25 - 4k. Step 3: So 4k = 24 and k = 6. Step 4: The polynomial becomes x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3), so the zeroes are 2 and 3. Step 5: Check: 3 - 2 = 1 as given, and 2 x 3 = 6 = k. Answer: k = 6 and the zeroes are 2 and 3.

boardQuestions.question: Find the zeroes of the polynomial 6x^2 - 7x - 3 and verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Split the middle term: 6x^2 - 9x + 2x - 3 = 3x(2x - 3) + 1(2x - 3) = (2x - 3)(3x + 1). Step 2: The zeroes are x = 3/2 and x = -1/3. Step 3: Sum = 3/2 - 1/3 = (9 - 2)/6 = 7/6 and -b/a = -(-7)/6 = 7/6, verified. Step 4: Product = (3/2) x (-1/3) = -1/2 and c/a = -3/6 = -1/2, verified. Answer: the zeroes are 3/2 and -1/3, with both relationships verified.

boardQuestions.question: In a physics activity, a student throws a ball straight up and models its height (in metres) after t seconds by the quadratic polynomial h(t) = -5t^2 + 20t. The ball returns to the ground when the height becomes 0. (a) Find the zeroes of h(t) and state what they represent. (b) After how many seconds does the ball return to the ground? (c) Verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients of h(t).
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Solve -5t^2 + 20t = 0, that is -5t(t - 4) = 0, so the zeroes are t = 0 and t = 4. Step 2: t = 0 is the launch time and t = 4 is the landing time, so the ball returns to the ground after 4 seconds. Step 3: Sum of zeroes = 0 + 4 = 4 and -b/a = -20/(-5) = 4, verified. Step 4: Product = 0 x 4 = 0 and c/a = 0/(-5) = 0, verified. Answer: (a) the zeroes are 0 and 4, the launch and landing times, (b) the ball lands after 4 seconds, (c) both sum and product relationships are verified.

chapters.title: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
chapters.summary: A pair of linear equations ax + by + c = 0 represents two straight lines whose common point, if it exists, is the solution of the system. This chapter trains you to solve pairs graphically, by substitution and by elimination, to decide consistency using the ratios a1/a2, b1/b2 and c1/c2, and to convert word problems on ages, money, fractions and speeds into solvable systems.
hotTopics: Consistency conditions using a1/a2, b1/b2, c1/c2
Graphical method and number of solutions
Substitution and elimination methods
Value of k for unique, no or infinite solutions
Word problems on ages, fractions and money
Boat, stream and two-digit number problems

sections.heading: Pair of Linear Equations and Their Solutions
points: A linear equation in two variables is ax + by + c = 0 where a and b are not both zero; a pair is a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 together with a2x + b2y + c2 = 0.
A solution is a pair (x, y) satisfying both equations simultaneously; geometrically it is a common point of the two lines.
Three outcomes exist: the lines intersect at one point (exactly one solution), coincide (infinitely many solutions), or are parallel (no solution).
Consistency test by ratios: if a1/a2 is not equal to b1/b2, there is a unique solution; if a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2, infinitely many; if a1/a2 = b1/b2 but this is not equal to c1/c2, no solution.

Worked mini-example: for x + 2y - 4 = 0 and 2x + 4y - 12 = 0, a1/a2 = 1/2, b1/b2 = 2/4 = 1/2, c1/c2 = 4/12 = 1/3; the a and b ratios match but the c ratio does not, so the lines are parallel and there is no solution.

keyTerms.meaning: A pair with at least one solution (unique or infinitely many).
A pair with no solution, shown by parallel lines.
The same line written twice; every point of the line is a solution.

sections.trick: ABC rule: arrange both equations as ax + by + c = 0, compare the ratios of a, b, c in order, and let the first mismatch tell the story: unique, infinite or none.
sections.examPointer: A 1-2 mark question almost always asks the number of solutions or a value of k for a given outcome; write all three ratios before stating the conclusion.

sections.heading: Graphical Method of Solving
points: Draw each equation as a straight line by finding two or three points that satisfy it, then read the solution from the graph.
The point where the two lines cross gives the unique solution; parallel lines give no solution; the same line drawn twice gives infinitely many solutions.

Worked mini-example with steps: solve x + y = 5 and x - y = 1 graphically. Step 1: the first line passes through (5, 0) and (0, 5). Step 2: the second line passes through (1, 0) and (0, -1). Step 3: the lines cross at (3, 2), so x = 3, y = 2. Step 4: check 3 + 2 = 5 and 3 - 2 = 1.
Always verify the graphical answer by substituting into both equations.
Choose points far apart to draw accurate lines, and read the intersection carefully to the nearest half unit on your grid.

keyTerms.meaning: The single common point of two crossing lines, which is the solution of the system.
The points where a line crosses the axes, used to draw it quickly.

sections.trick: Intercept shortcut: for ax + by = c, plot (c/a, 0) and (0, c/b); joining them gives an accurate line in seconds.
sections.examPointer: Graph questions carry separate marks for the table of points, the drawn lines and the written answer; never skip the final verification line.

sections.heading: Substitution Method
points: Solve one equation for one variable, substitute that expression into the other equation, and solve the resulting one-variable equation.

Worked example with steps: solve 3x + 4y = 10 and 2x - 2y = 2. Step 1: from the second equation x = y + 1. Step 2: substitute into the first: 3(y + 1) + 4y = 10. Step 3: 7y + 3 = 10 gives y = 1, and then x = 2. Step 4: check 3(2) + 4(1) = 10 and 2(2) - 2(1) = 2.
Substitution is fastest when one variable has coefficient 1 or -1, since no fractions appear.
If the substituted equation loses both variables and gives a true statement like 0 = 0, the system has infinitely many solutions; a false one like 0 = 5 means no solution.
Write the final answer as an ordered pair (x, y) and substitute back into the equation you did not use, to verify.

keyTerms.meaning: Replacing a variable by an equivalent expression derived from the other equation.
A statement like 0 = 0 (infinite solutions) or 0 = 5 (no solution) that appears when both variables vanish.

sections.trick: Pick the variable with coefficient 1 to express first; it avoids fractions entirely and speeds up the algebra.
sections.examPointer: When the question names the method, show the substitution line explicitly; the marks are for the process, not just the final pair.

sections.heading: Elimination Method
points: Multiply one or both equations by suitable non-zero numbers so that one variable has equal or opposite coefficients, then add or subtract to eliminate that variable.

Worked example with steps: solve 3x + 4y = 10 and 2x - 2y = 2 by elimination. Step 1: multiply the second equation by 2: 4x - 4y = 4. Step 2: add to the first: 7x = 14, so x = 2. Step 3: substitute into 2x - 2y = 2 to get y = 1. Step 4: check 3(2) + 4(1) = 10.
Elimination is preferred when substitution would create fractions.
If both variables vanish giving 0 = 0, the equations are dependent with infinitely many solutions; 0 = non-zero means the system is inconsistent.
Keep signs tidy: subtracting means subtracting every term, including the constants.

keyTerms.meaning: Removing one variable by making its coefficients equal and adding or subtracting the equations.
A rescaled pair of equations having exactly the same solution set.

sections.trick: LCM trick: multiply each equation by the other equation's coefficient of the variable you want to kill; the coefficients become equal automatically.
sections.examPointer: Questions often allow any method, but the safest for 3-markers is elimination followed by one verification line at the end.

sections.heading: Word Problems on Linear Pairs
points: Translate the story into two equations by naming the unknowns (say x and y), solve the pair, and answer in context with units.
Age problems: use present ages as variables; future or past ages are formed by adding or subtracting years on both sides.
Fraction problems: let the fraction be x/y; conditions on the numerator and denominator give two linear equations.
Money and cost problems: totals and differences of quantities give the two equations directly.

Worked mini-example with steps: the sum of two numbers is 25 and their difference is 5. Step 1: x + y = 25 and x - y = 5. Step 2: adding gives 2x = 30, so x = 15. Step 3: then y = 10. Answer: the numbers are 15 and 10.

keyTerms.meaning: Translating a word situation into equations and interpreting the solution back in context.
The unknowns x and y defined from the story, always with units attached.

sections.trick: Fix the units first (rupees, years, km/h) and let the smaller quantity be y; this halves the sign errors.
sections.examPointer: Five-mark word problems award marks for defining variables, forming both equations, solving and writing the concluding statement; the final line (hence the numbers are...) carries marks.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Exam Tips (Linear Equations)
points: Mistake: comparing ratios without arranging the equations as ax + by + c = 0; move every term to the left first, including the constant.
Mistake: dropping signs while shifting terms, so c1/c2 comes out wrong and the consistency conclusion flips.
Mistake: in elimination, subtracting only the variable terms and ignoring the constants.
Mistake: solving a word problem correctly but never answering the actual question asked (age, speed, fraction or cost).
Tip: for unique, no or infinitely many solutions, always quote the ratio condition as the justification.
Tip: use substitution when a coefficient is 1 and elimination otherwise; verify every answer by substituting into the equation you did not use.

keyTerms.meaning: Having at least one solution; both unique-solution and infinite-solution systems are consistent.
Having no solution, displayed by parallel lines and unequal c ratios.

sections.trick: Unique-None-Infinite in ratio language: a and b ratios unequal = unique; a and b equal but c different = none; all three equal = infinite.
sections.examPointer: Case-study questions wrap a linear system in a shopping or trip story; extracting the two equations itself carries marks, so write them clearly before solving.

mcqs.question: The solution of the equations x + y = 10 and x - y = 2 is:
mcqs.explanation: Adding the equations gives 2x = 12, so x = 6 and then y = 4; check 6 + 4 = 10 and 6 - 4 = 2.

mcqs.question: If a1/a2 is not equal to b1/b2 for a pair of linear equations, then the lines are:
mcqs.explanation: Unequal a and b ratios guarantee exactly one intersection point, which gives the unique solution.

mcqs.question: The pair x + 2y - 4 = 0 and 2x + 4y - 12 = 0 has:
mcqs.explanation: a1/a2 = 1/2, b1/b2 = 2/4 = 1/2, c1/c2 = 4/12 = 1/3; the a and b ratios match but the c ratio does not, so the lines are parallel and there is no solution.

mcqs.question: The pair x + y = 3 and 2x + 2y = 6 has:
mcqs.explanation: The second equation is the first multiplied by 2, so the lines coincide: a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2 = 1/2 gives infinitely many solutions.

mcqs.question: For what value of k do the equations 2x + 3y = 4 and kx + 6y = 8 have infinitely many solutions?
mcqs.explanation: Infinitely many solutions need a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2; here 2/k = 3/6 = 4/8 = 1/2, so 2/k = 1/2 gives k = 4.

mcqs.question: For what value of k will the equations x + 2y = 3 and 5x + ky = 7 have no solution?
mcqs.explanation: No solution needs a1/a2 = b1/b2 but this ratio must not equal c1/c2; 1/5 = 2/k gives k = 10, and indeed 1/5 is not equal to 3/7.

mcqs.question: The sum of two numbers is 25 and their difference is 5. The numbers are:
mcqs.explanation: Adding x + y = 25 and x - y = 5 gives 2x = 30, so x = 15 and y = 10; check 15 + 10 = 25 and 15 - 10 = 5.

mcqs.question: The system 3x + y - 1 = 0 and kx + 3y - 2 = 0 has a unique solution when:
mcqs.explanation: A unique solution needs a1/a2 not equal to b1/b2, that is 3/k not equal to 1/3, which fails only when k = 9; so the condition is k not equal to 9.

mcqs.question: A fraction becomes 2/3 when 1 is added to both its numerator and denominator, and becomes 1/2 when 1 is subtracted from both. The fraction is:
mcqs.explanation: Let the fraction be x/y: (x + 1)/(y + 1) = 2/3 gives 3x - 2y = -1, and (x - 1)/(y - 1) = 1/2 gives 2x - y = 1; solving gives x = 3, y = 5; check 4/6 = 2/3 and 2/4 = 1/2.

mcqs.question: A boat covers 30 km upstream and 44 km downstream in 10 hours, and 40 km upstream and 55 km downstream in 13 hours. The speed of the boat in still water and the speed of the stream are:
mcqs.explanation: Let the upstream and downstream speeds be u and v: 30/u + 44/v = 10 and 40/u + 55/v = 13 give u = 5 and v = 11; then the still water speed = (5 + 11)/2 = 8 km/h and the stream speed = (11 - 5)/2 = 3 km/h.

boardQuestions.question: Solve the pair of equations x + y = 14 and x - y = 4.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Add the two equations: (x + y) + (x - y) = 14 + 4, so 2x = 18 and x = 9. Step 2: Substitute into x + y = 14: y = 14 - 9 = 5. Step 3: Check: 9 - 5 = 4. Answer: x = 9 and y = 5.

boardQuestions.question: Find the value of k for which the equations kx + 3y = 3 and 12x + ky = 6 have no solution.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Write in standard form: kx + 3y - 3 = 0 and 12x + ky - 6 = 0. Step 2: No solution needs a1/a2 = b1/b2 but this ratio must not equal c1/c2. Step 3: k/12 = 3/k gives k^2 = 36, so k = 6 or k = -6. Step 4: Also k/12 must not equal 3/6 = 1/2, so k cannot be 6. Step 5: Hence k = -6. Answer: k = -6.

boardQuestions.question: Solve by the substitution method: 3x + 4y = 10 and 2x - 2y = 2.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: From 2x - 2y = 2, we get x = y + 1. Step 2: Substitute into 3x + 4y = 10: 3(y + 1) + 4y = 10. Step 3: 7y + 3 = 10 gives y = 1. Step 4: Then x = 1 + 1 = 2. Step 5: Check in the first equation: 3(2) + 4(1) = 10. Answer: x = 2 and y = 1.

boardQuestions.question: Solve the equations 2x + 3y = 11 and 2x - 4y = -24, and hence find the value of m for which y = mx + 3.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Subtract the second equation from the first: (2x + 3y) - (2x - 4y) = 11 - (-24), so 7y = 35 and y = 5. Step 2: Substitute into 2x + 3y = 11: 2x + 15 = 11, so x = -2. Step 3: Put x = -2 and y = 5 into y = mx + 3: 5 = -2m + 3, so m = -1. Step 4: Check the second equation: 2(-2) - 4(5) = -4 - 20 = -24. Answer: x = -2, y = 5 and m = -1.

boardQuestions.question: The age of a father is twice the sum of the ages of his two children. After 20 years, his age will be equal to the sum of the ages of his children. Find the present age of the father.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Let the father's present age be x years and the sum of the children's present ages be y years. Step 2: The first condition gives x = 2y. Step 3: After 20 years the father is x + 20 and the children's ages add to y + 40, so x + 20 = y + 40. Step 4: Substitute x = 2y: 2y + 20 = y + 40, so y = 20. Step 5: Then x = 40. Step 6: Check: after 20 years the father is 60 and the children's ages add to 20 + 40 = 60. Answer: the present age of the father is 40 years.

boardQuestions.question: The sum of a two-digit number and the number formed by reversing its digits is 66. If the digits of the number differ by 2, find the number. How many such numbers are there?
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Let the tens digit be a and the units digit be b, so the number is 10a + b. Step 2: Adding the reversed number: 10a + b + 10b + a = 11(a + b) = 66, so a + b = 6. Step 3: The digits differ by 2: a - b = 2 (taking a as the larger digit). Step 4: Adding gives 2a = 8, so a = 4 and b = 2, giving the number 42. Step 5: Reversing the roles, a = 2 and b = 4 gives 24, which also satisfies both conditions since 24 + 42 = 66 and the digits differ by 2. Answer: the numbers are 42 and 24, so there are exactly two such numbers.

boardQuestions.question: For the annual sports day, a school orders t-shirts and caps from a supplier. It pays Rs 1200 for 2 t-shirts and 3 caps, and Rs 1300 for 3 t-shirts and 2 caps. (a) Form a pair of linear equations for this situation. (b) Find the cost of one t-shirt and one cap. (c) Find the total cost of 5 t-shirts and 4 caps.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Let one t-shirt cost Rs x and one cap cost Rs y. Step 2: The equations are 2x + 3y = 1200 and 3x + 2y = 1300. Step 3: Multiply the first by 3 and the second by 2: 6x + 9y = 3600 and 6x + 4y = 2600. Step 4: Subtract: 5y = 1000, so y = 200. Step 5: Substitute into 2x + 3y = 1200: 2x + 600 = 1200, so x = 300. Step 6: Cost of 5 t-shirts and 4 caps = 5(300) + 4(200) = 1500 + 800 = Rs 2300. Answer: (a) 2x + 3y = 1200 and 3x + 2y = 1300, (b) one t-shirt costs Rs 300 and one cap costs Rs 200, (c) the total cost is Rs 2300.

chapters.title: Quadratic Equations
chapters.summary: Any equation that can be reduced to the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a not 0 is a quadratic equation. This chapter covers solving by factorisation and by the quadratic formula, analysing the discriminant b^2 - 4ac to decide the nature of the roots, and modelling word problems on numbers, ages, areas and speeds where a quadratic equation is formed and the meaningful root is selected.
hotTopics: Factorisation by splitting the middle term
Quadratic formula and discriminant
Nature of roots (D greater than, equal to, less than 0)
Value of k for equal roots
Word problems on numbers, ages and area
Speed and time word problems

sections.heading: Standard Form of a Quadratic Equation
points: A quadratic equation is ax^2 + bx + c = 0 where a, b, c are real numbers and a is not 0; if a = 0 the equation becomes linear.
To identify one, expand every bracket, bring all terms to one side, and check that the degree is exactly 2 after simplification.
Example: x + 1/x = 3 (x not 0) becomes x^2 - 3x + 1 = 0 after multiplying by x, so it is quadratic.
Counter-example: (x - 2)^2 = x^2 simplifies to x^2 - 4x + 4 = x^2, that is -4x + 4 = 0, so it is linear, not quadratic.
The values of x satisfying the equation are called its roots (the same idea as zeroes); a quadratic equation has at most two roots.

keyTerms.meaning: An equation reducible to ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a not 0.
A value of x that satisfies the equation; a quadratic has at most two roots.

sections.trick: Expand and cancel before deciding: the x^2 term must survive with a non-zero coefficient for the equation to be quadratic.
sections.examPointer: One-mark checks ask whether a given equation is quadratic; always show the simplified form as justification rather than guessing.

sections.heading: Solution by Factorisation
points: Split the middle term bx into two terms whose coefficients multiply to a x c and add to b.

Worked example with steps: solve 2x^2 + 7x + 5 = 0. Step 1: find two numbers with product 2 x 5 = 10 and sum 7; they are 2 and 5. Step 2: split the middle term: 2x^2 + 2x + 5x + 5 = 0. Step 3: group: x(2x + 5) + 1(2x + 5) = 0, so (2x + 5)(x + 1) = 0. Step 4: the roots are x = -5/2 and x = -1.
If the product ac is positive, both split numbers carry the sign of b; if ac is negative, the two numbers have opposite signs.
Roots can be zero or negative; a root x = k means the factor (x - k) appears in the factorisation.
Always substitute one root back into the original equation as a quick check.

keyTerms.meaning: Writing bx as a sum of two terms chosen so that factor-by-grouping becomes possible.
If a product of factors equals 0, at least one factor must be 0.
The two numbers whose product is ac and whose sum is b.

sections.trick: Find the magic pair: product ac, sum b; write them as coefficients of x, then factor by grouping. If no pair appears quickly, switch to the formula.
sections.examPointer: When the question specifies factorisation and the numbers turn ugly, show two honest attempts and then finish with the formula; CBSE rewards correct method identification.

sections.heading: Quadratic Formula
points: For ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (a not 0) the roots are x = (-b + sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/(2a) and x = (-b - sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/(2a); this is the quadratic formula, also called the Sridharacharya rule.
The quantity D = b^2 - 4ac is the discriminant; it sits inside the square root and decides everything about the roots.

Worked example with steps: solve 2x^2 - 7x + 3 = 0. Step 1: D = (-7)^2 - 4 x 2 x 3 = 49 - 24 = 25. Step 2: sqrt(D) = 5. Step 3: x = (7 + 5)/4 = 3 or x = (7 - 5)/4 = 1/2. Step 4: check 2(3)^2 - 7(3) + 3 = 18 - 21 + 3 = 0.
Reduce the equation to standard form first, then identify a, b, c with their signs before substituting.
The formula works for every quadratic, even when factorisation is difficult, provided D is not negative.

keyTerms.meaning: x = (-b + sqrt(D))/(2a) and x = (-b - sqrt(D))/(2a) with D = b^2 - 4ac.
The expression D = b^2 - 4ac that classifies the roots of a quadratic equation.
The traditional Indian name for the quadratic formula.

sections.trick: Singsong memory: minus b, plus-minus, root of b-square minus four-a-c, all over two-a; write D first and the rest follows.
sections.examPointer: Three-markers often command the phrase by using the quadratic formula; write D, then the formula, then both roots, since skipping the D line costs marks.

sections.heading: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
points: If D = b^2 - 4ac > 0, the equation has two distinct real roots.
If D = 0, it has two equal real roots, both equal to -b/(2a).
If D < 0, there are no real roots (the roots are not real numbers).
Worked mini-example: for 2x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0, D = 16 - 24 = -8 < 0, so no real roots exist.
To find k for equal roots, set b^2 - 4ac = 0 and solve for k; for distinct roots set D > 0, and for no real roots set D < 0.

keyTerms.meaning: Two different real roots, arising when D > 0.
Both roots identical and equal to -b/(2a), arising when D = 0.
The case D < 0, where the square root of a negative number is needed.

sections.trick: D decides: D positive = two different, D zero = twins, D negative = none.
sections.examPointer: A favourite 2-marker asks the nature of roots without solving; a 3-marker asks for k making the roots equal by putting b^2 = 4ac.

sections.heading: Word Problems Based on Quadratic Equations
points: Form the equation from the story, solve it, then reject any root that contradicts the physical situation (negative length, negative age).
Number problems: consecutive integers x and x + 1 lead to equations like x^2 + (x + 1)^2 = given sum of squares.
Age, area and speed problems follow the same pattern; speed-time problems often give equations after converting time differences.

Worked mini-example with steps: two consecutive positive integers have squares adding to 365. Step 1: x^2 + (x + 1)^2 = 365. Step 2: 2x^2 + 2x - 364 = 0, so x^2 + x - 182 = 0. Step 3: (x + 14)(x - 13) = 0 gives x = 13 (reject x = -14). Answer: the integers are 13 and 14.
State the final answer as a sentence with units; the rejected root with one line of reason earns the last mark.

keyTerms.meaning: A root that also fits the physical conditions of the story.
A mathematically valid root that must be discarded in context, usually a negative length or age.

sections.trick: Ask of every root: can this be negative in real life? If not, reject it and write one line saying why.
sections.examPointer: Five-mark word problems give method marks for defining the variable, forming the equation, solving correctly and the final statement with the rejected root explained.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Exam Tips (Quadratic Equations)
points: Mistake: applying the formula without reducing to standard form, so b and c carry wrong signs.
Mistake: writing the formula with denominator a instead of the full 2a.
Mistake: saying no solution when D < 0; the precise statement is no real roots.
Mistake: in word problems, accepting a negative root blindly instead of rejecting it with a reason.
Tip: memorise the three discriminant cases with one example of each (D > 0, D = 0, D < 0).
Tip: after factorising, expand the factors mentally to confirm the middle term matches before writing the roots.

keyTerms.meaning: ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with every term on the left and a not 0.
Computing b^2 - 4ac to classify the roots before solving.

sections.trick: Before the formula, list a, b, c with signs in a row (a = 2, b = -7, c = 3); this single habit removes most sign errors.
sections.examPointer: Expect one find-k discriminant question and one full word problem; both reward a neat standard form and a verification line.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a quadratic equation?
mcqs.explanation: Multiplying x + 1/x = 3 by x gives x^2 - 3x + 1 = 0, which is quadratic; (x - 2)^2 = x^2 reduces to -4x + 4 = 0, which is linear, and the others are cubic and linear.

mcqs.question: The roots of the equation x^2 = 36 are:
mcqs.explanation: x^2 = 36 gives x = 6 or x = -6, since both 6^2 and (-6)^2 equal 36.

mcqs.question: The discriminant of 2x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0 is:
If x = 2 is a root of x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0, the other root is:
mcqs.explanation: The product of the roots is c/a = 6, so the other root = 6/2 = 3; indeed x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3).

mcqs.question: The roots of x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0 are:
mcqs.explanation: Split the middle term: x^2 - 2x - 3x + 6 = x(x - 2) - 3(x - 2) = (x - 2)(x - 3), so x = 2 or x = 3.

mcqs.question: The equation 2x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0 has:
mcqs.explanation: D = (-4)^2 - 4 x 2 x 3 = 16 - 24 = -8 < 0, so the equation has no real roots.

mcqs.question: The equation 2x^2 + kx + 3 = 0 has two equal roots when k equals:
mcqs.explanation: Equal roots need k^2 - 4 x 2 x 3 = 0, so k^2 = 24 and k = 2sqrt(6) or k = -2sqrt(6).

mcqs.question: The number that must be added to x^2 - 8x to make it a perfect square is:
mcqs.explanation: Half of 8 is 4 and 4^2 = 16; then x^2 - 8x + 16 = (x - 4)^2 is a perfect square.

mcqs.question: Two positive numbers differ by 5 and their product is 50. The larger number is:
mcqs.explanation: Let the numbers be x and x - 5: x(x - 5) = 50 gives x^2 - 5x - 50 = 0 = (x - 10)(x + 5), so x = 10; check 10 - 5 = 5 and 10 x 5 = 50.

mcqs.question: The roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (a not 0) are reciprocals of each other when:
mcqs.explanation: If the roots are r and 1/r, their product is 1; since the product of roots = c/a, we need c/a = 1, that is c = a.

boardQuestions.question: Find the value of k for which the equation x^2 - 4x + k = 0 has two equal roots.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Equal roots need the discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac = 0. Step 2: Here a = 1, b = -4 and c = k. Step 3: D = 16 - 4k = 0. Step 4: So k = 4. Answer: k = 4.

boardQuestions.question: Without solving, state the nature of the roots of the equation x^2 - 6x + 9 = 0.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Here a = 1, b = -6 and c = 9. Step 2: D = b^2 - 4ac = 36 - 36 = 0. Step 3: Since D = 0, the equation has two equal real roots, each equal to -b/(2a) = 6/2 = 3. Answer: the equation has two equal real roots, both equal to 3.

boardQuestions.question: Solve 2x^2 - 7x + 3 = 0 by using the quadratic formula.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Here a = 2, b = -7 and c = 3. Step 2: D = (-7)^2 - 4 x 2 x 3 = 49 - 24 = 25. Step 3: sqrt(D) = 5. Step 4: x = (-b + sqrt(D))/(2a) = (7 + 5)/4 = 3 or x = (7 - 5)/4 = 1/2. Step 5: Check: 2(3)^2 - 7(3) + 3 = 18 - 21 + 3 = 0. Answer: the roots are 3 and 1/2.

boardQuestions.question: Find two consecutive positive integers, the sum of whose squares is 365.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Let the integers be x and x + 1. Step 2: x^2 + (x + 1)^2 = 365 gives 2x^2 + 2x + 1 = 365, so 2x^2 + 2x - 364 = 0. Step 3: Dividing by 2: x^2 + x - 182 = 0. Step 4: Factorising, (x + 14)(x - 13) = 0, so x = 13 or x = -14. Step 5: Reject x = -14 since the integers must be positive. Answer: the integers are 13 and 14, and 13^2 + 14^2 = 169 + 196 = 365.

boardQuestions.question: The perimeter of a rectangular field is 82 m and its area is 400 m^2. Find its length and breadth.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Let the length be l m and the breadth be b m; then 2(l + b) = 82 gives l + b = 41, and lb = 400. Step 2: So l and b are the roots of t^2 - 41t + 400 = 0. Step 3: D = 41^2 - 4 x 400 = 1681 - 1600 = 81 and sqrt(D) = 9. Step 4: t = (41 + 9)/2 = 25 or t = (41 - 9)/2 = 16. Step 5: Hence the length is 25 m and the breadth is 16 m. Step 6: Check: 2(25 + 16) = 82 and 25 x 16 = 400. Answer: the field measures 25 m by 16 m.

boardQuestions.question: A cottage industry produces a certain number of toys in a day. The cost of production of each toy (in rupees) was 5 more than the number of toys produced that day, and the total cost of production was Rs 750. Find the number of toys produced and the cost of each toy.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Let the number of toys be n, so the cost of each toy is Rs (n + 5). Step 2: The total cost gives n(n + 5) = 750. Step 3: So n^2 + 5n - 750 = 0. Step 4: Factorising, n^2 + 30n - 25n - 750 = n(n + 30) - 25(n + 30) = (n + 30)(n - 25) = 0, so n = 25 or n = -30. Step 5: Reject n = -30 since the number of toys cannot be negative. Answer: 25 toys were produced and each toy cost Rs 30, since 25 x 30 = 750.

boardQuestions.question: A stationery shop owner buys a batch of identical pens for Rs 600 to resell. He calculates that if each pen had cost him Rs 5 less, he could have bought 10 more pens for the same amount of money. (a) Form the quadratic equation for this situation. (b) Find the price he actually paid for each pen. (c) How many pens did he buy, and how many could he have bought at the lower price?
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: Let the actual price per pen be Rs p, so he bought 600/p pens. Step 2: At Rs (p - 5) each he could buy 10 more pens: 600/(p - 5) = 600/p + 10. Step 3: Multiplying throughout by p(p - 5): 600p = 600(p - 5) + 10p(p - 5). Step 4: Simplifying: 600p = 600p - 3000 + 10p^2 - 50p, so 10p^2 - 50p - 3000 = 0, that is p^2 - 5p - 300 = 0. Step 5: Factorising, (p - 20)(p + 15) = 0, so p = 20, rejecting p = -15 since a price cannot be negative. Step 6: He bought 600/20 = 30 pens; at Rs 15 each he could buy 600/15 = 40 pens, which is exactly 10 more. Answer: (a) p^2 - 5p - 300 = 0, (b) Rs 20 per pen, (c) 30 pens actually bought and 40 pens possible at the lower price.

chapters.title: Arithmetic Progressions
chapters.summary: An arithmetic progression is a list of numbers in which each term is obtained by adding a fixed number d to the previous term. The chapter develops the nth term formula a + (n - 1)d and the sum formula n/2[2a + (n - 1)d], applies them to find missing terms and sums, and closes with real-life word problems on savings, stacked logs and taxi fares.
hotTopics: nth term of an AP
Common difference and AP identification
Sum of the first n terms
Finding the number of terms from sum conditions
Word problems based on AP
Middle term and last term tricks

sections.heading: Introduction to Arithmetic Progressions
points: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a list of numbers in which each term is obtained by adding a fixed number d, called the common difference, to the term before it.
The general form is a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, ... where a is the first term and d = a_n - a_(n-1) is the common difference.
The common difference d may be positive (increasing AP like 2, 5, 8), negative (decreasing AP like 20, 15, 10) or zero (constant AP like 7, 7, 7).
A list is an AP only if every consecutive difference is the same; check at least two gaps before declaring it an AP.
Worked mini-example with steps: is 1, 4, 7, 10 an AP? Step 1: 4 - 1 = 3. Step 2: 7 - 4 = 3. Step 3: 10 - 7 = 3. All gaps equal 3, so it is an AP with a = 1 and d = 3.

keyTerms.meaning: A list of numbers with a fixed difference d between consecutive terms.
The fixed gap d = a_n - a_(n-1), which may be positive, negative or zero.

sections.trick: Same gap every time is an AP; if the gap itself changes (like 2, 4, 8), the list is not an AP.
sections.examPointer: One-mark questions test whether a given list is an AP or ask for d; show two consecutive subtractions for a safe two-line answer.

sections.heading: The nth Term of an AP
points: Formula: a_n = a + (n - 1)d, where a is the first term and d the common difference.
The nth term from the end is l - (n - 1)d where l is the last term; for an AP of N terms, the last term is l = a + (N - 1)d.
Worked example with steps: find the 10th term of the AP 2, 7, 12, ... Step 1: a = 2 and d = 5. Step 2: a_10 = 2 + (10 - 1) x 5 = 2 + 45 = 47. Answer: 47.
To find which term equals a given value x, set a + (n - 1)d = x and solve for n; n must come out as a positive integer.
If the nth term is given as an expression in n, such as a_n = 3n + 2, the common difference is a_n - a_(n-1), which is the coefficient of n.

keyTerms.meaning: The term in position n, given by a_n = a + (n - 1)d.
The term counted backwards, equal to l - (n - 1)d where l is the last term.
A formula in n that produces every term of the AP.

sections.trick: Term = first term + gap x (position minus 1): a + (n - 1)d; the (n - 1) is the classic slip, so say minus one aloud.
sections.examPointer: Which term of the AP ... is 78? is a 2-mark staple; set the nth term equal to the value, solve for n, and answer as it is the 16th term.

sections.heading: Sum of First n Terms
points: Formula: S_n = n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d].
Equivalent form: S_n = n/2 (a + l), where l is the last term; the sum is half of (first plus last) times the number of terms.
When S_n is given and the number of terms is unknown, the equation is quadratic in n; it may give two valid answers or one after rejecting a meaningless value.
Worked example with steps: find the sum of the first 20 terms of the AP 1, 4, 7, ... Step 1: a = 1, d = 3, n = 20. Step 2: S_20 = 20/2 [2 x 1 + 19 x 3] = 10 x 59 = 590. Answer: 590.
Special cases: the sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n + 1)/2, the sum of the first n odd numbers is n^2, and the sum of the first n even numbers is n(n + 1).

keyTerms.meaning: The sum S_n of the first n terms of the AP.
The final term actually being added, so that S_n = n/2 (a + l).

sections.trick: Gauss pairing trick: first + last, second + second-last all equal the same total, so the sum is (number of pairs) x that total = n/2 (a + l).
sections.examPointer: Sum questions in boards almost always need the bracket form n/2[2a + (n - 1)d]; write a, d, n in a row before substituting to earn the method mark.

sections.heading: Working Between S_n, a_n and the Terms
points: Key identity: a_n = S_n - S_(n-1) for n > 1, and a_1 = S_1.
If S_n is given as a formula, find a_n by subtraction and then check whether the resulting list is an AP.
The middle term of an AP with an odd number N of terms is the (N + 1)/2-th term.
Three-term trick: take the terms as a - d, a, a + d so that the sum is 3a; four terms: a - 3d, a - d, a + d, a + 3d so that the sum is 4a.

Worked mini-example with steps: if S_n = 3n^2 + 5n, then a_1 = S_1 = 8, a_2 = S_2 - S_1 = 22 - 8 = 14, a_3 = S_3 - S_2 = 42 - 22 = 20; the differences 6 and 6 are equal, so the AP is 8, 14, 20 with common difference 6.

keyTerms.meaning: a_n = S_n - S_(n-1) for n > 1, with a_1 = S_1.
The central term of an AP with an odd number of terms.

sections.trick: If S_n is a quadratic in n with no constant term, the list is an AP whose common difference is twice the coefficient of n^2; here 2 x 3 = 6.
sections.examPointer: Questions hand you S_n and ask for the nth term or the AP itself; the subtraction a_n = S_n - S_(n-1) is the whole trick, so show it explicitly.

sections.heading: Word Problems Based on AP
points: Money saved with fixed monthly increases, salaries with annual increments, fares with fixed per-km charges and stacked logs all form arithmetic progressions.
Read the story to fix a (the first term) and d (the increase per step); the number of steps is n.

Worked mini-example with steps: 200 logs are stacked with 20 logs in the bottom row, 19 in the next row, and so on; in how many rows is the pile complete? Step 1: the rows are 20, 19, 18, ... so a = 20 and d = -1. Step 2: S_n = n/2 [40 - (n - 1)] = n(41 - n)/2 = 200. Step 3: n^2 - 41n + 400 = 0 gives n = 16 or 25. Step 4: n = 25 would need negative log counts, so n = 16 rows. Answer: 16 rows, with 5 logs in the top row.
Fare problems: the fare for n kilometres often has the form a + (n - 1)d with a the first slab charge.
Always connect the answer back to the story with units (rows, rupees, kilometres).

keyTerms.meaning: Mapping a story onto a (first term), d (step) and n (number of steps).
The value of n that keeps every term of the AP physically valid.

sections.trick: Bottom row = a, each step up = d (usually negative), total = S_n; the phrase in how many rows, months or years means solve for n.
sections.examPointer: Five-mark application questions expect the equation in n, the rejection of the impossible root, and a concluding sentence that also computes the last term or the total.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Exam Tips (AP)
points: Mistake: using a + nd instead of a + (n - 1)d; the (n - 1) is the single most common AP error.
Mistake: after getting two values of n from a sum equation, forgetting to check which value is meaningful.
Mistake: writing S_n = n/2 (a + l) with l taken from a different number of terms; l must be the last term actually summed.
Mistake: assuming the list is an AP without verifying that the consecutive differences are equal.
Tip: for which term questions, the answer is the term number n, not the value of the term.
Tip: memorise the three quick sums: naturals n(n + 1)/2, odd numbers n^2, even numbers n(n + 1).

keyTerms.meaning: The position n of a term in the AP, always a positive integer.
Writing a + nd instead of the correct a + (n - 1)d.

sections.trick: Before substituting, chant: a, d, n. Identify all three, then choose a_n or S_n.
sections.examPointer: Boards pair one find-the-term 2-marker with one find-the-sum 3-marker; a clean substitution with a, d, n listed earns the method mark even if the arithmetic slips.

mcqs.question: The common difference of the AP 3, 7, 11, 15, ... is:
mcqs.explanation: d = 7 - 3 = 4, and 11 - 7 = 4 confirms the gap is constant.

mcqs.question: The 10th term of the AP 2, 7, 12, ... is:
The sum of the first 10 natural numbers is:
Which of the following lists is an AP?
mcqs.explanation: 5, 10, 15, 20 has a constant difference of 5; the first has gaps 3, 5, 7, the second has doubling gaps, and the fourth has unequal gaps.

mcqs.question: Which term of the AP 3, 8, 13, 18, ... is 78?
If the nth term of an AP is 7 - 4n, its common difference is:
mcqs.explanation: d = a_n - a_(n-1) = (7 - 4n) - (7 - 4(n - 1)) = -4; also a_1 = 3 and a_2 = -1 confirm the difference -4.

mcqs.question: The sum of the first 20 terms of the AP 1, 4, 7, ... is:
The middle term of the AP 6, 13, 20, ..., 216 is:
mcqs.explanation: 6 + (n - 1) x 7 = 216 gives n = 31 terms; the middle term is the 16th, equal to 6 + 15 x 7 = 111.

mcqs.question: How many terms of the AP 24, 21, 18, ... must be taken so that their sum is 78?
mcqs.explanation: S_n = n/2 [48 - 3(n - 1)] = 78 gives n^2 - 17n + 52 = 0 = (n - 4)(n - 13), so n = 4 or n = 13; both work because the terms from the 5th to the 13th (12, 9, 6, 3, 0, -3, -6, -9, -12) add to 0.

mcqs.question: 56 is divided into four parts forming an AP such that the ratio of the product of the first and fourth parts to the product of the second and third parts is 5 : 6. The parts are:
mcqs.explanation: Let the parts be a - 3d, a - d, a + d, a + 3d; the sum 4a = 56 gives a = 14; then (196 - 9d^2)/(196 - d^2) = 5/6 gives 1176 - 54d^2 = 980 - 5d^2, so 49d^2 = 196 and d = 2; the parts are 8, 12, 16, 20.

boardQuestions.question: Find the 20th term of the AP 10, 7, 4, ...
Which term of the AP 21, 18, 15, ... is -81?
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: a = 21 and d = -3. Step 2: Setting a + (n - 1)d = -81 gives 21 - 3(n - 1) = -81. Step 3: So 3(n - 1) = 102, giving n - 1 = 34 and n = 35. Step 4: Check: 21 + 34 x (-3) = 21 - 102 = -81. Answer: -81 is the 35th term.

boardQuestions.question: Find the sum of the first 22 terms of the AP 8, 3, -2, ...
How many two-digit numbers are divisible by 6?
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: The two-digit multiples of 6 run from 12 to 96 and form the AP 12, 18, 24, ..., 96. Step 2: Here a = 12, d = 6 and a_n = 96. Step 3: 12 + (n - 1) x 6 = 96 gives (n - 1) x 6 = 84, so n - 1 = 14 and n = 15. Answer: there are 15 such numbers.

boardQuestions.question: The sum of the 4th and 8th terms of an AP is 24 and the sum of the 6th and 10th terms is 44. Using the formula for the nth term, find the first three terms of the AP.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: a_4 + a_8 = (a + 3d) + (a + 7d) = 2a + 10d = 24, so a + 5d = 12. Step 2: a_6 + a_10 = (a + 5d) + (a + 9d) = 2a + 14d = 44, so a + 7d = 22. Step 3: Subtracting gives 2d = 10, so d = 5. Step 4: Then a = 12 - 25 = -13. Step 5: Check: a_4 = -13 + 15 = 2 and a_8 = -13 + 35 = 22, sum 24; a_6 = -13 + 25 = 12 and a_10 = -13 + 45 = 32, sum 44. Answer: the first three terms of the AP are -13, -8 and -3.

boardQuestions.question: 200 logs are stacked in the following way: 20 logs in the bottom row, 19 in the next row, 18 in the row above it and so on. In how many rows is the stack complete, and how many logs are there in the top row?
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: The rows form the AP 20, 19, 18, ... with a = 20 and d = -1. Step 2: The total is S_n = n/2 [2 x 20 + (n - 1)(-1)] = n(41 - n)/2, and this equals 200. Step 3: So n^2 - 41n + 400 = 0, giving (n - 16)(n - 25) = 0, that is n = 16 or n = 25. Step 4: For n = 25 the upper rows would need a negative number of logs, so n = 16 is the valid answer. Step 5: The top row contains 20 + 15 x (-1) = 5 logs. Answer: the stack is complete in 16 rows, with 5 logs in the top row.

boardQuestions.question: A city taxi charges Rs 60 for the first kilometre and Rs 15 for each additional kilometre. Ravi notices the fares for successive kilometre slabs form a list. (a) Show that the fares for 1 km, 2 km, 3 km, ... form an AP and write its common difference. (b) What is the fare for a 12 km ride? (c) Ravi paid Rs 615 for one ride; how far did he travel?
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: The fares are Rs 60 for 1 km, Rs 75 for 2 km, Rs 90 for 3 km, and each term increases by Rs 15; hence the list is an AP with a = 60 and d = 15. Step 2: (b) The fare for 12 km = a + (12 - 1)d = 60 + 11 x 15 = 60 + 165 = Rs 225. Step 3: (c) Solve 60 + (n - 1) x 15 = 615. Step 4: (n - 1) x 15 = 555 gives n - 1 = 37, so n = 38. Answer: (a) the fares form an AP with common difference Rs 15, (b) the 12 km fare is Rs 225, (c) the ride was 38 km long.

chapters.title: Triangles
chapters.summary: Two figures of the same shape but not necessarily the same size are similar. This chapter proves the Basic Proportionality (Thales) theorem and its converse, establishes the similarity criteria AA, SSS and SAS, links the areas of similar triangles to the square of the side ratio, and proves the Pythagoras theorem with its converse, making it the classic proof chapter of the board exam.
hotTopics: BPT (Thales) theorem and its proof
Converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem
AA, SSS and SAS similarity criteria
Areas of similar triangles
Pythagoras theorem and its proof
Converse of the Pythagoras theorem

sections.heading: Similar Figures and Similar Triangles
points: Two figures are similar if they have the same shape: corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio (proportional).
All circles, all squares and all equilateral triangles are similar to one another; two arbitrary triangles are similar only if both the angle and side conditions hold.
Notation: triangle ABC ~ triangle DEF means A corresponds to D, B to E and C to F; the order of letters carries the correspondence, so ratios must be read in that order.
Congruent triangles are the special case of similar triangles with scale factor 1 : 1.
Corresponding altitudes, medians and angle bisectors of similar triangles are in the same ratio as the corresponding sides.

keyTerms.meaning: Figures with equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.
The agreed pairing of vertices, written through the order of letters.

sections.trick: Shape same, size may differ; always write the correspondence order first, then build ratios along that order.
sections.examPointer: One to two mark questions give two triangles with a letter order and ask which criterion proves similarity; read the letter order before writing any ratio.

sections.heading: Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales) and Its Converse
points: BPT statement: if a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides at distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.
In triangle ABC with DE parallel BC, where D lies on AB and E on AC: AD/DB = AE/EC; also AD/AB = AE/AC and DB/AB = EC/AC.
Converse: if a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.
Memory line: parallel sides cut proportional pieces; equal ratios on two sides force parallelism.

Proof outline: join BE and CD, draw EN perpendicular to AB and DM perpendicular to AC; then AD/DB = area(ADE)/area(BDE) and AE/EC = area(ADE)/area(CDE); but area(BDE) = area(CDE) since both stand on base DE between the same parallels DE and BC, hence AD/DB = AE/EC.

Worked mini-example with steps: D and E on AB and AC with DE parallel BC, AD = 4 cm, DB = 6 cm, AE = 5 cm. Step 1: AD/DB = 4/6 = 2/3. Step 2: AE/EC must also equal 2/3, so 5/EC = 2/3. Step 3: EC = 7.5 cm.

keyTerms.meaning: A line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally.
Equal ratios on two sides of a triangle force the joining line to be parallel to the third side.
Segments whose lengths are in the same ratio.

sections.trick: Say it twice before every proof: BPT means parallel sides cut proportional pieces.
sections.examPointer: The 5-mark state and prove BPT question appears regularly; the proof uses areas of triangles on the same base between the same parallels, so practise the construction lines.

sections.heading: Criteria for Similarity of Triangles
points: AA (or AAA) criterion: if two angles of one triangle are equal to two angles of another triangle, the triangles are similar.
SSS criterion: if the corresponding sides of two triangles are proportional, the triangles are similar.
SAS criterion: if one angle of a triangle equals one angle of another and the sides including these angles are proportional, the triangles are similar.
Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides; areas scale by the square of the side ratio.

Worked mini-example with steps: in triangles ABC and PQR, angle A = angle P, angle B = angle Q, AB = 6 cm, PQ = 9 cm, BC = 8 cm. Step 1: two pairs of equal angles give similarity by AA. Step 2: AB/PQ = BC/QR, so 6/9 = 8/QR. Step 3: QR = 12 cm. Answer: QR = 12 cm.

keyTerms.meaning: Two pairs of equal angles prove similarity.
Proportional corresponding sides prove similarity.
One equal angle with proportional including sides proves similarity.

sections.trick: Angle-angle is enough: two pairs of equal angles lock the third pair automatically because angles sum to 180 degrees.
sections.examPointer: Three-mark questions give a figure with some sides and angles, ask you to prove two triangles similar and then find a missing side; name the criterion before writing the ratios.

sections.heading: Areas of Similar Triangles
points: Theorem: the ratio of the areas of two similar triangles equals the square of the ratio of their corresponding sides.
So area ratio = (AB/PQ)^2 = (BC/QR)^2 = (CA/RP)^2, and the same square relation holds for corresponding altitudes, medians and perimeters.

Worked mini-example with steps: the areas of two similar triangles are 49 cm^2 and 81 cm^2. Step 1: the side ratio is sqrt(49) : sqrt(81) = 7 : 9. Step 2: the triangle with area 49 has corresponding sides 7/9 of the other triangle. Answer: corresponding sides are in the ratio 7 : 9.
To compare areas from sides, square the ratio; to compare sides from areas, take the square root.
Board questions chain this theorem with a similarity proof: prove similarity first, then convert the area statement into a length statement.

keyTerms.meaning: Areas of similar triangles are in the square of the ratio of corresponding sides.
The constant ratio of corresponding sides of similar triangles.
Perpendiculars from matching vertices; they follow the same ratio as the sides.

sections.trick: Areas go as squares: sides double means area four times; to go from area back to side, take the square root.
sections.examPointer: A 3-5 mark favourite gives two areas and one side of the smaller triangle and asks for the matching side of the bigger one; take square roots carefully and label which triangle is which.

sections.heading: Pythagoras Theorem and Its Converse
points: Pythagoras statement: in a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides; in triangle ABC right-angled at B, AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2.

Proof idea: draw BD perpendicular to AC. Triangles ABD and ABC are similar (AA), giving AB^2 = AD x AC; triangles BCD and ABC are similar, giving BC^2 = DC x AC; adding, AB^2 + BC^2 = AC(AD + DC) = AC^2.
Converse: if in a triangle the square of one side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, the angle opposite the first side is a right angle.

Worked mini-example with steps: a ladder 25 m long leans against a wall with its foot 7 m from the wall. Step 1: the hypotenuse is 25 and the base is 7, with height h on the wall. Step 2: h^2 = 25^2 - 7^2 = 625 - 49 = 576. Step 3: h = 24 m. Answer: the ladder reaches 24 m up the wall.
Converse in action: sides 6, 8, 10 satisfy 6^2 + 8^2 = 10^2, so the angle between the sides of length 6 and 8 is a right angle.

keyTerms.meaning: The longest side of a right triangle, opposite the right angle.
If a^2 + b^2 = c^2 for the side lengths of a triangle, the triangle is right-angled opposite the side c.
A triangle with one angle exactly 90 degrees.

sections.trick: The biggest side is the suspect hypotenuse; test a^2 + b^2 against c^2 to decide whether the angle is right or not.
sections.examPointer: The 5-mark Pythagoras proof written with Given, To Prove, Construction and Proof blocks is a board classic; practise the perpendicular construction BD to AC.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Exam Tips (Triangles)
points: Mistake: mismatching correspondence; if triangle ABC ~ triangle EDF, then AB/ED is the correct ratio, not AB/DE.
Mistake: using BPT when the line is not given parallel, or claiming parallelism without first proving equal ratios (the converse needs the ratio condition).
Mistake: setting the area ratio equal to the side ratio instead of its square.
Mistake: applying Pythagoras in a triangle that has not been shown right-angled; prove or cite the converse first.
Tip: board proofs need the format Given, To Prove, Construction (if any), Proof, Conclusion; missing blocks cost marks.
Tip: in every similarity proof, name the criterion (AA, SSS or SAS) explicitly before writing the side ratios.

keyTerms.meaning: The labelled structure CBSE expects in geometry proofs.
Corresponding Parts of Similar Triangles are proportional; the working rule after similarity is proved.

sections.trick: Proof skeleton for BPT: join BE and CD, drop perpendiculars EN and DM, use equal areas on the common base DE, cancel and conclude AD/DB = AE/EC.
sections.examPointer: Triangles is the proof chapter: expect one 3-marker application and one 5-mark theorem proof; write statements in words, not just ratios.

mcqs.question: Two triangles are similar if their corresponding angles are ___ and their corresponding sides are ___.
mcqs.explanation: Similarity means the same shape: equal angles with sides in a constant ratio.

mcqs.question: If AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD, then triangle ABC and triangle DEF are similar by the:
mcqs.explanation: All three pairs of corresponding sides are proportional, which is exactly the SSS similarity criterion.

mcqs.question: The Basic Proportionality Theorem says that a line parallel to one side of a triangle, meeting the other two sides, divides them:
options: in a ratio equal to the base
mcqs.explanation: If DE is parallel to BC in triangle ABC, then AD/DB = AE/EC: the two sides are cut proportionally.

mcqs.question: If two similar triangles have corresponding sides in the ratio 1 : 2, the ratio of their areas is:
mcqs.explanation: The area ratio is the square of the side ratio: (1/2)^2 = 1/4.

mcqs.question: In triangle ABC, D and E lie on AB and AC with DE parallel to BC. If AD = 4 cm, DB = 6 cm and AE = 5 cm, then EC equals:
mcqs.explanation: By BPT, AD/DB = AE/EC, so 4/6 = 5/EC gives EC = 5 x 6/4 = 7.5 cm.

mcqs.question: Triangles ABC and DEF are similar with AB = 6 cm, DE = 9 cm and BC = 8 cm. Then EF equals:
mcqs.explanation: AB/DE = BC/EF gives 6/9 = 8/EF, so EF = 8 x 9/6 = 12 cm.

mcqs.question: If two angles of one triangle are equal to two angles of another triangle, the triangles are similar by the:
mcqs.explanation: Two pairs of equal angles force the third pair to be equal (angle sum 180 degrees), so the triangles are similar by AA.

mcqs.question: A ladder 25 m long leans against a vertical wall with its foot 7 m from the wall. The height reached on the wall is:
